newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand seeks warmer defence ties with U.S.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand seeks warmer defence ties with U.S.

text.p: New Zealand's Prime Minister Jim Bolger, keen to build on improving relations with Washington, on Wednesday called for closer collaboration with the United States in multinational defence training.

In the prepared text of a speech to the American Chamber of Commerce here, Bolger said a better defence relationship could also open the way for New Zealand to consider more spending on defence equipment.

"A shift in U.S. attitudes toward exercising and training involving our two countries' defence forces in a multi-lateral setting would better enable New Zealand defence forces to make a continued contribution in the international arena," he said.
He explained there was increasing pressure on his four-month-old coalition government to lift funding in defence, "particularly in the capital area".
"That extra investment may be justified, but not in isolation of other moves in our wider international defence relationships," Bolger said.
Wellington's political and security relationship with the United States suffered for a period of about 10 years after the country introduced anti-nuclear laws in 1985.
However, it has improved steadily during the past two years.
This week New Zealand, as one of the members of the Five Power Defence Arrangement (FPDA) which does not include the U.S., is taking part in air and naval exercises off Malaysia.
On Tuesday all five participating countries' defence ministers said they welcomed a continued U.S. presence in Asia.
